prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological classification of insulators, and for its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are a new class of quantum matter defined by band topology and protected edge and surface states, and the quantum spin Hall effect gave the idea a concrete, measurable form. The chain is the one I trust most: a decisive prediction (Kane and Mele, with the Z2 classification), a clean transport observation (Molenkamp's HgTe wells, 2007), and then roughly two decades of independent confirmation in InAs/GaSb, in three-dimensional materials and by ARPES, where theory and spectroscopy agree quantitatively. It has changed how the community classifies electronic phases, it is routinely taught, and it is not premature. Kane-Mele-Molenkamp is the compact theory-plus-experiment configuration, with the three-name limit respected.
statement.case_against: The attribution is genuinely contestable. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp's group to look in HgTe is not among the credited names, and the 3D generalisation (Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents, Roy) lies partly outside the slate. The 2016 prize to Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz covers topological phases and could be read as overlap. Several colleagues rank this lower than I do (Olsson sixth, Lindroth fourth). Practical payoffs such as dissipationless edge transport and topological quantum computing remain unrealised, though that should not weigh against a discovery prize.

responses.point: Olsson calls the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang a serious attribution issue that may mean the three names do not represent who did the original work, and notes partial overlap with the 2016 prize. She ranks the candidate sixth.
responses.response: I take the BHZ point seriously and it is the strongest reservation I have. But the Kane-Mele 2005 papers came first and carry the QSH concept and the Z2 invariant, and the HgTe observation is Molenkamp's experimental achievement. The citation can be worded around the prediction of the effect and its observation, which lets us name BHZ's contribution in the scientific background without crediting them. On 2016, Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz honoured topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall precursors, not time-reversal-invariant topological insulators. I would accept that the allocation is imperfect, but not that it is disqualifying, since every candidate on the slate has some outside-the-list credit. I also do not think her first choice, B046, is stronger on this axis, since Krivanek's absence is a comparable gap.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B061 second and calls it a clean, general idea with decisive experimental confirmation and enormous influence. He places the Toner-Tu-Vicsek active-matter theory first, on the grounds that it is a simple mechanism behind a messy phenomenon.
responses.response: I agree with his assessment of B061, including that Haldane's 2016 prize helps rather than hurts, and I am glad of the support. On B008 I respect the conceptual elegance and the long-range-order result in two dimensions, but I am not persuaded that it is as ready as topological insulators. As he concedes, the quantitative Toner-Tu exponents are not cleanly confirmed in experiment, and I am the member who asks how robust a result is and whether it has been independently confirmed. It is also supported by only one opening ballot. I would be glad to hear what quantitative experimental tests he would regard as decisive. If they are convincing I could move B008 up my alternates, but for now I do not.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a clear, original strong light-matter coupling result that underpins superconducting quantum processors, and she flags that she is close to this community and may be biased. She ranks B061 third and defers to condensed-matter colleagues.
responses.response: Her case for cQED is strong, and I ranked it fifth for a reason of timing, not quality. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close enough that the committee would have to explain that cQED is a distinct discovery, and Girvin's absence from the credited names weakens the allocation more than the topological-insulator gap does, because he is a decisive architect of the proposal. She is right to flag her own proximity; I would suggest we treat that candidly. As the 2025 chair I would resist a back-to-back award in the same device area unless the committee is clear on why. I appreciate her third place for B061 and her point that the question there is credit, not worth.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the optical lattice clock first as precision atomic physics at its best, and rates B061 fourth, deferring to condensed-matter colleagues and noting that Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Fu-Kane-Moore are not credited.
responses.response: Her case for B040 is convincing and, since it is the one candidate that most of the committee ranks highly, I regard it as the main competitor. I ranked it eighth only because it is outside my expertise, and I defer to her and Kroll on priority between the Tokyo and JILA efforts. Where I disagree is on the weight of the overlap with 2005 and 2012. I do not see that as decisive, but I would want an explanation of why this is a discovery of physics and not an instrument advance, given that the redefinition of the second has not yet taken place. I would be comfortable with it as the other half of a prize or as my first alternative. On her attribution concern for B061, I would answer that no 3D name is required, since the citation is about the QSH state.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first and B017 (atom interferometry) second, on the view that progress is limited by what we can measure and how precisely, and notes that the prior 2005 and 2012 prizes cover adjacent ground.
responses.response: I accept the measurement-first philosophy, and I value the quantitative control, which is the same thing I look for in electronic-structure work, but it describes one kind of discovery. Topological insulators were a conceptual surprise that experiments confirmed, and they deserve a place on the same footing. I would raise a concern about B017: he himself calls attribution crowded and historically contested, with several near-simultaneous 1991 demonstrations and Chu outside the slate. Credit ambiguity of that kind seems at least as bad as the BHZ problem for B061, so I do not think it should be ranked ahead of B061 for attribution reasons.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp allocation given that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D pioneers are outside the credited names.
Whether partial overlap with the 2016 topological-phases prize is read as duplication or as natural continuation.
Whether B040 (Katori and Ye) has such broad support that it should be preferred over B061 on consensus grounds, given that I cannot judge priority details in atomic physics.
Whether the 2025 prize on circuit quantum tunnelling makes B055 too close in time.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the credited names Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori, Ye or Hosono. I have a general, non-personal connection to the field of correlated and topological materials as a theorist, and I chaired the 2025 committee, which awarded the circuit tunnelling prize, which is relevant to B055 but not a personal conflict.
